Revenue can rise while the owner’s surplus falls: chart the unit sales needed after a price cut

Separate revenue, variable costs and fixed costs, then compare operating break-even with the higher volume needed to preserve an original monthly surplus.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a lower unit price with the extra volume needed to preserve monthly operating surplus

Interactive planning lab

Original monthly operating surplus before owner transfers and tax$1,500
Comparison monthly operating surplus after the price cut$500
Minimum whole monthly units to preserve the original surplus200

Original hypothetical one-product monthly cost-volume model. Variable cost per unit is calculated from the entered share of the original price, then held at $60.00 through the discount comparison; it is not recalculated as that share of the lower price. The new unit selling price is $80.00 and contribution per new unit is $20.00. Fixed operating costs stay unchanged. The minimum whole-unit volume to meet or exceed the original surplus is 200. This exceeds the separately entered capacity of 180 units. All selected sales are collected and their variable costs paid in the same month. No sales tax, income tax, debt service, new equipment, inventory timing, receivable delay, extra staffing, tiered costs, demand response or owner withdrawal is included. Operating surplus is not after-tax household income or proof that cash is freely distributable. The volume target preserves the original surplus, which can itself be negative; it is different from breaking even at zero profit. No actual price, capacity or demand estimate is supplied.

The central idea

A lower price reduces the contribution on every unit already being sold. Compare the additional units at the new contribution per unit before carrying a revenue increase into the household income plan.

01

A household supported by a small business needs more than a revenue target

A successful-looking promotion can sell more units and collect more revenue while leaving less to support the owner. The missing link is the contribution left after the variable cost of each sale.

The U.S. Small Business Administration’s break-even guide separates unit selling price, variable costs and fixed costs in a one-product calculation. BDC’s break-even explanation also distinguishes the sales level needed to cover costs from a wider analysis of price and volume. These sources support the framework; every business amount and sales case here is invented.

The tool compares two monthly operating plans for one product or standard service unit. It assumes every selected sale is collected and its variable cost is paid in the same month. It does not predict how customers respond to a price or certify that the selected volume can be achieved.

02

Calculate what each original unit contributes before fixed costs

The original price is CAD 100 per unit. The variable-cost input is 60% of that original price, producing a cash cost of CAD 60 per unit. This cost is then held fixed during the discount comparison. It is not recalculated as 60% of the discounted selling price.

Each original sale contributes CAD 100 − CAD 60 = CAD 40 toward monthly fixed costs and surplus. At 100 units, revenue is CAD 10,000, variable costs are CAD 6,000 and contribution is CAD 4,000.

Subtracting the unchanged CAD 2,500 of fixed operating costs leaves CAD 1,500 of monthly operating surplus. That is before owner transfers and income tax, with financing, equipment spending and working-capital timing outside this simplified model.

The distinction matters because a dollar of revenue is not a dollar available to spend at home. Variable costs need to be funded first, and fixed costs still need to be covered.

03

A 20% price cut halves this example’s contribution per unit

The entered 20% cut lowers the selling price from CAD 100 to CAD 80. Since the same unit still costs CAD 60, its contribution falls from CAD 40 to CAD 20. A 20% reduction in the selling price has produced a 50% reduction in contribution per unit.

The selected comparison sells 150 units, 50% more than before. Revenue becomes CAD 12,000, a 20% increase. Variable costs become CAD 9,000, a 50% increase, because they follow the unit count at the unchanged CAD 60 cost.

Only CAD 3,000 of contribution remains. After the same CAD 2,500 fixed costs, operating surplus is CAD 500, down CAD 1,000 or about 66.67% from the original CAD 1,500. The first chart puts revenue and both cost categories beside each other so that the stronger revenue headline does not hide the weaker surplus.

The two unit counts are independent scenario inputs. Their comparison does not estimate that a 20% price cut will cause a 50% volume increase.

04

Preserving revenue, breaking even and preserving surplus are three different targets

At CAD 80 per unit, preserving the original CAD 10,000 revenue requires 125 units. Those sales produce 125 × CAD 20 = CAD 2,500 of contribution, exactly equal to the fixed operating costs. The operating surplus is zero.

Thus 125 units is also this discounted case’s operating break-even point. It covers the modeled costs but does not preserve the owner’s original CAD 1,500 surplus.

To keep that original surplus with unchanged fixed costs, contribution must remain CAD 4,000. The required volume is CAD 4,000 ÷ CAD 20 = 200 units. The business must double its original unit sales, rather than merely increase volume by 20% or match the old revenue.

More generally, with positive contribution per discounted unit, the comparison target is original units × original contribution per unit ÷ new contribution per unit. The headline rounds that result upward to a whole unit. A fractional calculated equality may be useful on the curve, but a whole-unit sales plan must meet or exceed it.

05

Check the volume target against capacity before treating it as household income

The separately entered capacity is 180 units per month. The 200-unit target exceeds it. At 180 units and the discounted CAD 20 contribution, the operating surplus would be 180 × CAD 20 − CAD 2,500 = CAD 1,100, still CAD 400 below the original plan.

The selected 150-unit comparison fits within that capacity, but fitting within capacity does not prove demand exists. Conversely, a case above the entered limit is flagged as arithmetic that is not feasible under that capacity assumption.

Expanding capacity could require more staff, space, equipment or other spending. Those changes would invalidate the assumption of unchanged fixed and per-unit costs. The model does not add them automatically or assume that capacity can be raised without cost.

The volume curve and matrix therefore remain conditional comparisons. Points or cells beyond the entered capacity are not sales forecasts. Their role is to expose the scale of the required change.

06

Reconcile the change in surplus without counting the interaction twice

The waterfall starts with the original CAD 1,500 surplus. First, applying the CAD 20 price reduction to the original 100 units removes CAD 2,000. Then the additional 50 units contribute 50 × CAD 20 = CAD 1,000 at the new margin. The endpoint is CAD 500.

Using the old CAD 40 contribution for those extra units would overstate their benefit. They are sold at the reduced price too. The bridge’s order keeps that price-volume interaction inside the new contribution used for the volume change.

A different decomposition order could assign the interaction to a different step while reaching the same final surplus. The chart is an exact accounting explanation of two entered cases, not evidence that one action caused a particular customer response.

07

More units cannot repair a non-positive contribution per unit

With the original CAD 100 price and CAD 60 variable cost, a 40% price cut leaves a CAD 60 selling price and zero contribution. No number of those sales produces the original CAD 4,000 contribution. Fixed costs still leave an operating loss of CAD 2,500.

A larger cut puts the selling price below the unchanged variable cost. Each additional sale then reduces the modeled surplus. When original contribution is positive and discounted contribution is zero or negative, the tool reports no finite volume that preserves the original surplus instead of displaying an artificial huge target.

With zero original sales, there is no original contribution to preserve; zero comparison units meet that baseline. Also, preserving an original negative surplus does not make a business profitable. These boundary cases are reasons to keep the target definition visible.

08

Carry a supported cash amount into the household plan

Before relying on a promotion to support personal spending, check the actual price, unit costs, fixed costs, realistic demand and operational capacity over the same period. Separate costs that change with volume from costs that remain fixed only within a relevant range.

This tool excludes sales tax, income tax, debt payments, new equipment, extra staffing, inventory timing and unpaid customer invoices. Even its positive operating surplus is not automatically after-tax household income or cash available for an owner withdrawal.

The related business-cash guide follows stock, receivables and withdrawals; the contractor guide looks at billable capacity. Together, those questions help prevent a sales target from becoming a personal income assumption before the necessary costs, cash dates and constraints have been checked.
